data.title: Most Microsoft services in Sâpore restored after outage that lasted more than 24 hours
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Most e-mail services here have been restored on Nov 14, a day after a Microsoft outage that affected hundreds of thousands of users globally.

Various statutory boards and government agencies including the Inland Revenue Authority of Singapore, Singapore Land Authority, Singhealth and the Singapore Police Force noted in separate Facebook posts late on Nov 13 and on the morning of Nov 14 that their e-mail services are up and running.

Banks such as DBS, UOB and Maybank have also updated on their respective Facebook pages that their e-mail services have been restored.

Reports of issues with Microsoft Outlook peaked at 1,135 at about 9.30 am in Singapore on Nov 13, gradually falling to 347 at about 8.45 pm on the same day.

In a media reply on Nov 13, the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech) confirmed that some government systems were hit by the disruption, adding that it was working with Microsoft to restore the affected services.

The private and education sectors were also affected by the outage, with banks here reporting e-mail disruptions, though core banking operations were unaffected.

The e-mail services for Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) and the Singapore University of Social Sciences (SUSS) were also affected by the disruption.

The outage, reports of which started climbing around 5.25 pm GMT on Nov 12 (1.25 am on Nov 13, Singapore time) according to Ookla, is one of the longest in Microsoft’s history and the second disruption to its services in 2026, Reuters reported.

Microsoft said the outage specifically hit features tied to Exchange Online – its cloud-based e-mail and scheduling hub – leaving unconnected applications operational.

Reuters reported that Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels.

Microsoft said in an update posted on X at 12.40 am on Nov 14 that it saw “broad recovery and stability” across its services.

It clarified that the issue was not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.

“The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the post added.

Microsoft also said that it will provide a full post-incident report once its review is complete.

The Straits Times has contacted GovTech for more information. THE STRAITS TIMES

data.title: TikTok Shop is coming for Shopeeâs ecommerce crown
data.description:
IN THE second quarter of 2026, TikTok Shop overtook Shopee by sales volume in Thailand. While it was only a 3 per cent margin, it is a sign that Shopee’s dominance in South-east Asia is beginning to falter.

This could signal more intense competition in the region’s e-commerce sector next year, with TikTok Shop launching a standalone app. It also raises the question of where else Shopee could lose its lead, or if Thailand is an exception.

Analysts suggest Vietnam, where TikTok Shop is trailing closely behind Shopee in gross merchandise volume (GMV), could soon be next.

Toni Ruotanen, head of South-east Asia markets at marketing firm Havas, estimates that based on TikTok Shop’s current pace of growth, it could overtake Shopee in Vietnam within the next six to nine months.

In Vietnam, “TikTok Shop has already overtaken Shopee in the fashion category, while beauty is now evenly split between the two platforms,” Ruotanen tells Tech in Asia. He previously served as chief commercial officer at e-commerce enabler Crea.

TikTok’s Thailand edge

TikTok Shop had already overtaken Shopee in the skincare and face-care categories in Thailand six to 12 months before Q2 2026, notes Simon Torring, co-founder of markets insights firm Cube Asia. Because of this, TikTok catching up to Shopee was “not so unexpected,” he says.

According to Torring, Thailand’s e-commerce market is skewed towards certain product categories that TikTok Shop is a natural fit for.

Within South-east Asia, Thailand has the biggest beauty, personal care, and wellness market in e-commerce, with these categories accounting for around 30 per cent of the country’s online sales. These categories are well-suited to short videos and livestreams, where creators can demonstrate products, review them, and answer questions.

Paul Srivorakul, CEO of e-commerce enabler aCommerce, similarly notes that among the brands it works with, beauty and personal care were TikTok Shop’s leading categories in Thailand in the first half of 2026. ACommerce helps brands such as Estee Lauder and Unicharm manage their sales across multiple online platforms.

The relatively higher margins of beauty and personal care give brands more room to pay affiliate commissions to creators. Sales through affiliate marketing, driven by short-video and live content, account for roughly 32 per cent of TikTok Shop’s GMV in South-east Asia, according to Srivorakul.

Izhhar Gemilang, assistant manager for e-commerce at AB Foods, agrees that categories such as fashion, beauty, and snacks tend to perform better through TikTok Shop affiliates because those products are easier to demonstrate in a livestream.

AB Foods distributes products by Twinings and Ovaltine in Southeast Asia. Gemilang declined to share which e-commerce platform generated more sales for his company or which platform AB Foods invests more into.

Rather than any unique strategy it is employing in the market, Torring believes TikTok Shop’s success in Thailand largely comes from the country’s strong demand for categories that are better suited to its platform.

“I don’t expect that the investment level or the P&L health of TikTok Shop is dramatically different in Thailand from the other markets,” Torring says.

A TikTok spokesperson declined to comment.

TikTok Shop previously announced that it had trained local creators and 10,000 small and medium-sized enterprises in Thailand on livestreaming. In March, the platform said it had over three million sellers and more than five million creators in the country.

Will Vietnam follow suit?

Consumer spending on beauty and personal care products is increasing in Vietnam.

In 2025, e-commerce customers spent nearly 74.4 trillion dong (US$3 billion) on those categories, up almost 30 per cent from a year earlier, according to data platform Metric.vn.

In Q4 last year, TikTok Shop accounted for roughly half of beauty and personal care sales across e-commerce platforms in the country, narrowly ahead of Shopee’s 48 per cent.

Vietnam’s established creator ecosystem and rising consumer spending mean it can become another TikTok Shop stronghold in Southeast Asia. The country has “a few mega livestreamers” like Hannah Ohlala and Vo Ha Linh, who have 2.1 million and 5.6 million followers on TikTok, respectively.

These livestreamers yield large influence not just in the beauty category but also across products for women. Ohlala has driven more than 10 per cent of monthly beauty sales volume in Vietnam’s e-commerce market, Torring notes.

However, Havas’ Ruotanen says Vietnamese consumers are hesitant to buy products at higher price points. This could make promotions and sales events – which Shopee frequently relies on – more effective as a marketing strategy.

Singapore is harder to crack

In Singapore, Shopee still leads by a wide margin, holding a 52 per cent of market share as of 2025. It’s followed by Lazada at 36 per cent and TikTok Shop at 6 per cent, according to a report from Momentum Works.

Shopee’s continued dominance in the country can be attributed to consumer habits. Singapore has a stronger tradition of mall-based shopping, while livestream shopping and short-form entertainment are less established than in other South-east Asian markets.

Singapore also has an “underdeveloped influencer scene,” Torring points out.

Many brands are hesitant to invest in Singapore because of its small market, notes Havas’ Ruotanen, citing his conversations with brands. Investing in TikTok Shop involves more than advertising spend, as it also requires budgets for affiliate commissions, livestreaming, and content production. Brands need sufficient sales volume to justify these investments.

As a result, “brands might start the TikTok Shop journey outside Singapore and at a later stage address the market,” Ruotanen says.

Despite this, the high purchasing power among Singapore consumers makes it an attractive market, notes Gemilang of AB Foods. That said, consumers in the country have plenty of convenient offline options for categories such as FMCG and daily essentials.

TikTok Shop faces different obstacles in other Southeast Asian markets.

In Indonesia and the Philippines, logistics and fulfilment remain major challenges. In Malaysia, TikTok needs to expand beyond categories such as beauty, fashion, and FMCG to become more competitive, including in higher-value product categories such as electronics and gadgets, Ruotanen says.

Shopee fights back

Shopee is not sitting idle as TikTok Shop gains ground.

It continues to invest in entertainment, recently introducing microdrama content to entice users to spend more time on the platform. Viewers can earn loyalty points by watching microdramas and use those points for discounts on purchases.

The strategy attempts to replicate TikTok’s appeal as an entertainment platform, where consumers organically stumble across products to buy even without an intent to purchase.

However, changing user habits will take time, and Shopee may struggle to convince users to see it as an entertainment destination.

Ruotanen is doubtful that consumers will turn to Shopee for content, as their intent when opening the app is more focused on shopping than entertainment.

Rather than relying on vouchers, Shopee is leaning more onto its paid loyalty programme, which gives members a 4 to 6 per cent discount on purchases. The approach could encourage consumers to stick with Shopee rather than compare prices across platforms, a strategy Torring likens to Amazon Prime.

Indeed, Sea CEO Forrest Li said during the company’s Q3 2026 earnings call that ShopeeVIP membership had exceeded 21 million at the end of September, up 40 per cent from the previous quarter. ShopeeVIP members accounted for close to 25 per cent of Shopee’s GMV during the quarter.

Shopee is also investing in faster delivery, which Torring sees as an effort to increase GMV by capturing a share of offline retail spending. The platform’s instant and same-day delivery accounted for nearly 15 per cent of orders in Bangkok and surrounding areas, according to Li.

Still, defending its market position will come at a cost. Torring predicts Shopee will raise its take rates – the commissions it charges sellers – by 5 to 7 per cent next year, particularly in categories where it faces stronger competition from TikTok Shop.

He expects Shopee to channel much of that additional revenue into platform vouchers to keep prices competitive.

Shopee declined to comment. However, Sea’s management had noted during the earnings call that Shopee’s future monetisation improvements are expected to come from advertising rather than fixed commissions.

“I believe that Shopee sees South-east Asia as a cannot-lose region,” says Torring. “It will become more aggressive at fighting back.” TECH IN ASIA

data.title: Trump to raise nuclear-arms cuts with Putin, Xi on Thursday, White House says
data.description:
[WASHINGTON] US President Donald Trump will raise nuclear-arms reduction at a meeting in China next week with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the White House said on Friday (Nov 14).

“He will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokeswoman, said on a call with reporters. She added that the meeting would take place on Thursday in China.

Trump’s repeated insistence that the first-of-its-kind meeting of the three leaders focus on nuclear arms reductions has riled China, which is hosting a summit focused on trade and commerce. China has rebuffed attempts to talk about nuclear arms with Russia and the United States, which have the largest stockpiles of such weapons.

Putin, Xi and Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen. Trump is leaving on Monday for a four-day trip to Asia that also includes a stop in the Philippines.

“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior Trump administration official said regarding the nuclear issue. “This is a difficult topic for China to address, but we do think it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things.”

The official added: “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”

Beijing has for years resisted direct engagement with Washington about its nuclear programme, saying it is more appropriate for Russia and the US to speak directly because of their large arsenals.

Russia has the most stored nuclear warheads, followed by the United States and China, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty between the US and Russia expired this year.

It was not clear whether Russia or China intended to engage in a conversation about arms reductions with Trump.

The Chinese and Russian embassies in Washington did not immediately respond to emailed requests for comment.

Trump will also raise the US-Israeli war against Iran in the meeting but is not expected to raise Russia’s war in Ukraine, the official said.

The Republican president is not expected to have a one-on-one meeting with Putin or discuss Ukraine’s access to satellite communications service provided by Elon Musk’s SpaceX. Musk is joining Trump on the trip to China but will not attend his meeting with Xi and Putin, according to the official.

“We’ve had many meetings recently with the Russians, but China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” the person said.

Trump is also not expected to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his trip to Asia, according to the official. REUTERS

data.title: US lifts nationwide flight shutdown caused by communications failure
data.description:
[WASHINGTON] The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) lifted a nationwide ground stop on Friday (Nov 13) after a communications failure at air traffic control centers caused chaos at airports and triggered the longest nationwide shutdown since the Sep 11, 2001, attacks.

More than 4,700 flights were cancelled and 10,000 delayed on Friday, while another 700 had already been cancelled for Saturday, according to FlightRadar24. Aviation analysts said it could take days for airlines to restore their schedules after a nationwide grounding that lasted more than four hours.

The Department of Homeland Security said there were no signs the outage was caused by a cyberattack.

The failure is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset by equipment and communications problems, controller shortages and aging infrastructure.

The only other nationwide ground stop since the Sep 11 attacks came in January 2023, when the FAA halted domestic departures for around 90 minutes. REUTERS

data.title: Ex-Nvidia CEO misled top lawyer on affair with Chinese businesswoman, sources say
data.description:
[SAN FRANCISCO] Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang misled several of the company’s leaders, including general counsel Tim Teter and chief marketing officer Alison Wagonfeld, about the nature of his relationship with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, with whom he had an affair, according to two people familiar with the matter and internal correspondence reviewed by Reuters.

Reuters reviewed many exchanges from October on condition of not quoting verbatim from the messages. The news agency is the first to report on this correspondence.

On Thursday (Nov 12), Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO, a spectacular fall from the chip industry’s heights where he was a pioneer of technology central to the recent boom in artificial intelligence.

He apologised in a statement on Sunday for being unfaithful to his wife and for disappointing the company. His statement did not specifically name Alice Huang, a former top executive of Nvidia customer Megaspeed International, whom the US was investigating for potentially spying for China. Jensen Huang and Alice Huang share a last name but are not related.

The New York Times earlier this week reported Huang also had an extramarital relationship with an Nvidia employee, and Reuters reported on Thursday that Huang had another intimate relationship with a different Nvidia employee.

Teter did not respond to a request for comment. Wagonfeld did not immediately respond to a request for comment. A representative for ex-CEO Huang and an Nvidia spokesperson declined to comment. A phone call and e-mail to contact information listed on a business card for Alice Huang went unanswered.

During the autumn of 2025 and in October 2026, in response to press queries that drew some Nvidia leaders’ attention to his relationship with Megaspeed and Alice Huang, Huang at both times described their interactions as appropriate, the people said, speaking on the condition of anonymity. Reuters only reviewed messages from the exchanges in October, not the ones from 2025.

In two separate messages in October, Huang told Nvidia leaders, including Teter and Wagonfeld, that the interactions reflected standard business dealings with customers. In other messages, Huang affirmed the routine nature of his interactions with Megaspeed.

Nvidia’s Huang also discussed taking legal action against the NY Times after it published an article in October of last year that drew attention to his meetings in public with Alice Huang, the people said.

That article had prompted Jensen Huang to communicate with some Nvidia leaders in 2025 about their interactions, which he did not describe as an affair, the people said. Ultimately, neither Nvidia nor Huang filed a lawsuit against the paper. A spokesperson for the NY Times said the paper received no legal demand.

It is unclear when his relationship with Alice Huang became intimate. Photos posted online and verified by Reuters show them together in the US, China and elsewhere, dating as far back as December 2023.

On Nov 10, the independent members of Nvidia’s board said they hired Wall Street law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an independent investigation after the NY Times and Wall Street Journal reported on Huang’s relations with Alice Huang, as well as US authorities’ suspicions that she was spying for China. Beijing has denied she is a spy.

Reuters has not independently verified whether Alice Huang was working on behalf of the Chinese government.

Jensen Huang said in an interview with Bloomberg published on Oct 29 that the US government had not informed him about its suspicions regarding Alice Huang.

Nvidia’s stock has fallen more than 30 per cent since its Oct 6 closing high, erasing more than US$1.8 trillion from its market capitalisation. REUTERS

data.title: Stocks to watch: SIA, CDL, Sats, AEM, StarHub, NTT DC Reit, SBS Transit, Centurion
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 12):

Singapore Airlines (SIA) : The national carrier posted net profit of S$209.7 million for its second quarter ended Sep 30, up from S$52.4 million in the previous corresponding period. This was due to stronger operating profit and a lower share of losses from associate Air India. Revenue rose 14.3 per cent to a record S$5.6 billion, while operating profit rose 16.3 per cent to S$463.7 million from a year earlier. For the first half of FY2026, SIA’s net profit fell 43.9 per cent to S$133.9 million year on year. The board declared an interim ordinary dividend of S$0.02 a share and an interim special dividend of S$0.05 a share, bringing the total payout to S$0.07 a share. Shares of SIA closed 0.4 per cent or S$0.03 higher at S$7.17 on Wednesday, before the news.

City Developments Limited (CDL) : The property group said it expects to post a “significantly weaker” financial performance for its second half ending Dec 31. Certain capital-recycling deals that the group had earlier expected to materialise in the rest of FY2026 are now expected to be completed in FY2027, it said in a business update on Wednesday. The group is also currently undertaking valuations of its property portfolio, which it noted “may give rise to impairment losses”. Shares of CDL closed 1.2 per cent or S$0.09 lower at S$7.12 on Wednesday, before the update.

Sats : The air cargo handler and airline caterer posted a 2.8 per cent rise in net profit to S$81.1 million for its second quarter ended Sep 30, from S$78.9 million in the previous corresponding period. This was due to higher cargo and meal volumes and lower tax expenses, even as the Middle East conflict raised input costs and disrupted operations, it said on Wednesday. Earnings per share stood at S$0.054 for the quarter, up from S$0.053 the year before. Revenue for the quarter rose 9 per cent to S$1.71 billion, from S$1.57 billion. Shares of Sats closed 2.6 per cent or S$0.10 higher at S$4 on Wednesday, before the news.

AEM : The semiconductor equipment maker’s net profit surged more than 18-fold to S$73.4 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from S$4 million a year earlier. Revenue rose 57.2 per cent to S$452.1 million on stronger demand for semiconductor testing solutions. AEM raised its FY2026 revenue guidance to S$680 million to S$705 million, from S$630 million to S$680 million, and its earnings per share guidance to S$0.30 to S$0.33, from S$0.245 to S$0.275. Shares of AEM closed 3.1 per cent or S$0.21 higher at S$7.05 on Wednesday.

StarHub : The telco reported a 26.3 per cent dip in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) to S$72.1 million for the third quarter ended Sep 30, from S$97.8 million the prior year. Revenue rose to S$486.8 million, up 4.5 per cent from S$464.8 million previously. The telco said that despite rising revenue, Ebitda continued to decline because of lower gross profit, higher operating expenditure and lower income from other avenues. Shares of StarHub ended flat at S$1.04 on Wednesday.

NTT DC Real Estate Investment Trust (Reit) : The Reit on Wednesday posted a distribution per unit of US$0.0432 for the first half of FY2026/27, 10 per cent above its initial public offering projection, as net property income exceeded forecasts and net finance costs came in lower than expected. For the six months ended Sep 30, distributable income stood at US$45 million, against the projected US$40.9 million. Net property income was 4.9 per cent above projection at US$55.8 million, while gross revenue came in 2 per cent higher at US$119.8 million. Units of NTT DC Reit fell 2.2 per cent or US$0.02 to close at US$0.90 on Wednesday, before the news.

SBS Transit : The public transport operator posted a 35.5 per cent rise in net profit to S$19.6 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30, from S$14.5 million in the previous corresponding period. This was due to a S$13 million write-back of prior years’ Fuel Equalisation Fund provisions, which was included in the operating profit. Operating profit for the quarter rose 37.7 per cent to S$22.6 million, from S$16.4 million in the year-ago period. Revenue fell 1.1 per cent to S$382.1 million from a year earlier due to a lower bus service fee from the loss of the Tampines package, as well as lower rail grants and ridership. Shares of SBS Transit closed flat at S$3.56 on Wednesday.

Centurion : The accommodation provider reported a 35 per cent rise in revenue to S$280.1 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from S$208.3 million in the previous corresponding period. This was mainly due to the consolidation of Westlite Mandai and new operational beds in Singapore, as well as its Harum Megah portfolio in Malaysia and Epiisod Macquarie Park in Australia. Revenue for the third quarter ended Sep 30 rose 41 per cent to S$95.2 million, it said in a business update. Shares of Centurion fell 2.4 per cent or S$0.03 to close at S$1.21 on Wednesday.

data.title: Tesla says it is starting to sell Cybercabs for personal use
data.description:
TESLA invited select customers to place orders for the Cybercab, suggesting it is preparing to make its driverless car available to consumers.

The two-seat vehicle, which lacks a steering wheel and foot pedals, initially launched as part of Tesla’s robotaxi service in Austin. Now, the Cybercab will be available via limited release in supported service areas, the company announced Friday (Nov 13) on X.

It was not immediately clear what Tesla defined as personal use, or whether the Cybercabs will be restricted to the existing geofenced area in Austin, which currently is the only place where the autonomous vehicles are operating as robotaxis. The company had previously posted an interest form for fleet operators, but not for individual owners.

Matt Holm, president of the Tesla Austin’s Owners Club, posted screenshots of an e-mail showing he ordered the vehicle after he was invited to reserve a Cybercab for US$29,990, plus a US$299 monthly subscription required to operate the vehicle.

The Cybercab’s regulatory future remains uncertain. One day after the car debuted in September, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration opened a probe into the process and technical data Tesla relied on when the company self-certified the vehicles as compliant with all federal safety standards. BLOOMBERG

data.title: Issue 220: COP31âs electric dreams; Singapore tweaks green finance rules for data centres
data.description:
COP31

Aiming for a pragmatic electrification goal

Pragmatic or ineffective?

Negotiators are huddling in Turkey for this year’s United Nations climate conference under an atmosphere of muted expectations, as governments are too busy dealing with global turmoil to prioritise global warming.

The challenge is to find a common path towards credible long-term outcomes while addressing short-term needs so that climate progress is calibrated but not abandoned. This should mean continued commitment towards net-zero emissions while allowing flexibility on how to get there, prioritising renewable energy and grid improvements, and unlocking investments in climate adaptation and resilience.

Singapore Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu says that reaching a global agreement at the conference known as COP31 will be more difficult than in previous years.

“The headwind is getting stronger, not weaker,” she says.

Indeed, the war in Iran and the massive data centre build-out driven by artificial intelligence has placed energy security at the top of mind for most governments. While this has helped to spur interest in renewables, it has also extinguished plans to phase out coal in countries like Indonesia that have domestic sources of the high-carbon fuel.

The economic uncertainties brought about by a fractured global trade system and the energy-led inflationary shock have also dampened growth expectations and lowered fiscal headroom for climate-related spending and investment.

Under such circumstances, the joint presidents of COP31 – Turkey and Australia – are pushing for a “35-by-35” goal to raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity to at least 35 per cent by 2035, from about 20 per cent at the moment.

It’s a target seemingly picked because it seems easy to accept in the face of all these headwinds. After all, the International Energy Agency estimates that current policies are already on a trajectory to reach 29 per cent electrification by 2035, so while going for 35 per cent might take more effort, it is still somewhat feasible. The increasingly competitive pricing of electric vehicles and battery solutions, as well as the data centre boom, suggest that the world is already headed in the right direction.

The COP31 presidents are also suggesting that the target give parties the flexibility to decide the energy supply mix, which will allow countries at different stages of development and with different levels of resources to choose energy transition pathways most appropriate to their circumstances.

Therein lies the rub. Setting an electrification target without binding it to emissions reductions or a higher share of renewable generation risks creating a meaningless goal, because electrification supported by renewables generation has a substantially different impact on emissions reduction from electrification supported by fossil fuel generation. It’s like ordering a cake without specifying the occasion it’s meant to celebrate or the type of cake desired. You’ll get your cake, but it might not be the one you were hoping to eat.

The rigour of the 35-by-35 target is likely to be a source of much debate, but a pragmatic goal that nudges all countries in the right direction is better than no agreement. Nevertheless, there can be a fine line between a pragmatic consensus and a meaningless one. Negotiators will have to work for the former.

The first step is to connect electrification with emissions goals, because mitigating greenhouse gas emissions is ultimately the objective of the climate conference. Without that north star, an electrification target could end up going nowhere.

Low-carbon generation must be an integral part of electrification, although the pace at which the transition occurs could afford some flexibility to countries that need it. Many developing countries will fall into that category. However, COP31 needs to deliver better support for emerging and developing countries to build low-carbon electricity generation and to modernise and improve their grid infrastructure to handle the increased electricity demand and to firm their network to handle the intermittency of renewable energy.

The high curtailment rate of renewable energy in certain parts of China demonstrates the importance of upgrading electrical grids when renewable generation scales up. Grid modernisation is an important enabling investment even in electrification strategies that are still heavily reliant on coal or natural gas generation. That is because the grid will be able to handle more renewable power in the future.

Beyond electrification, COP31 needs to take steps towards raising investments in climate adaptation and resilience. The current expectation is that global warming will overshoot the 1.5 deg C threshold. Emerging and developed countries – such as those in South-east Asia – are especially vulnerable to disruptions from climate change. The adaptation investment gap remains significant and needs to be closed.

Being pragmatic should not mean becoming less ambitious. Rather, it should be about realigning ambitions towards more viable areas. Electrification is a fine goal in the current environment, but it should be aimed strategically.

Sustainable finance

Looking past data centres’ efficiency

Singapore’s sustainable finance eligibility criteria for data centres may have a blind spot when it comes to assessing a centre’s impact on surrounding communities and ecosystems.

An update to the Singapore-Asia Taxonomy for Sustainable Finance – which sets the conditions under which various economic activities can qualify for sustainable financing – includes revisions to criteria for data centres that better recognise trade-offs between power and water efficiency.

Data centres are either air-cooled or water-cooled. An air-cooled data centre can be very water-efficient but will be less efficient in its electricity usage; conversely, a water-cooled data centre consumes more water but is more efficient in its power usage.

A data centre development outside Singapore pursuing green financing under the earlier version of the Taxonomy had to meet the platinum rating under Singapore’s Green Mark Scheme for data centres with regard to power efficiency, as well as a single water efficiency hurdle.

The revised green financing criteria relaxes power efficiency requirements for data centres built with tighter water constraints, encouraging optimisation of resources instead of improving one aspect at the expense of the other.

But while the taxonomy ensures that data centres obtaining sustainable financing under its criteria are broadly efficient, it does not have a robust approach to address the external impact of data centres on their surroundings.

Consider recent negative news coverage of official investigations into Google’s felling of forests in Finland for its data centre, as well as NextDC’s delays to projects amid community protests in Australia. The fact is that a large data centre has a substantial impact on its surrounding environment and communities by virtue of the scale of its physical footprint, of its emissions and of its absolute consumption of resources, regardless of the data centre’s efficiency.

Some additional criteria worth considering could be requirements for environmental impact assessments or community engagement to be carried out and adjudicated, or compliance with local policies that adequately cover those impacts.

External impact presents a risk if not properly addressed. Investors holding what they think is a sustainable bond may find the funded project generating negative impact, which could affect the value of the asset.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Singtel, ST Engg, Genting, First Resources, Golden Agri, CDG, Bumitama, Food Empire
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Friday (Nov 13):

Singtel : The telecommunications giant on Friday posted a 55 per cent decline in net profit to S$1.54 billion for the first half-year ended September, from S$3.4 billion in the year-ago period. This was mainly due to the absence of S$2.21 billion in net exceptional gains recorded a year earlier from the partial sale of its stake in Airtel and the Intouch-Gulf Energy merger. Excluding exceptional items, underlying net profit rose 10 per cent to S$1.49 billion, from S$1.35 billion a year earlier. The company declared a 10 per cent higher interim dividend of S$0.09 per share. Singtel closed S$0.01 or 0.2 per cent higher at S$4.15 on Thursday.

ST Engineering : The technology and engineering group posted a 9 per cent year-on-year increase in revenue to S$3.4 billion for the third quarter ended September, from S$3.1 billion a year earlier, it said on Friday. It also declared a third-quarter interim dividend of S$0.05 per share, up from S$0.04 a year earlier. Together with its first- and second-quarter dividends of S$0.04 and S$0.05 per share, respectively, this brings the total dividend for the first nine months to S$0.14 per share. ST Engineering closed S$0.02 or 0.2 per cent higher at S$9.76 on Thursday.

Genting Singapore : The integrated resort operator posted a 42.2 per cent fall in net profit to S$54.7 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30, from S$94.6 million in the corresponding year-ago period. Revenue for the quarter fell 12.9 per cent to S$566.1 million, from S$649.8 million a year earlier. Gaming revenue at Resorts World Sentosa (RWS), the group’s Singapore integrated resort, dropped 21.7 per cent to S$315 million in Q3, from S$402.3 million in the year-ago period. Genting Singapore said that renewal works at RWS will constrain operating capacity through 2027. Genting Singapore closed Thursday at S$0.61, down S$0.005 or 0.8 per cent.

First Resources : The palm oil producer posted a 40.1 per cent rise in its underlying net profit to US$122.7 million for the third quarter ended Sep 30, from US$87.5 million a year ago. The increase was boosted by higher sales of palm oil products and fruit bunches harvested from oil palm plants, it said. Sales was up 24.9 per cent to US$578.6 million for the quarter, compared with US$463.3 million a year ago. The group said it expects demand for palm oil to remain supported by Indonesia’s biodiesel programme. Shares of First Resources closed flat at S$2.79 on Thursday.

Golden Agri-Resources : The palm oil company posted a net profit of US$162 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30, a 32 per cent increase from US$123 million in the previous quarter. The rise in net profit was due primarily to higher plantation output and investment income received in Q3 2026, the company said. Revenue for Q3 was up 3 per cent at US$3.5 billion on a quarterly basis, supported by an appreciation in crude palm oil prices. Its shares ended Thursday 1.9 per cent or S$0.005 higher at S$0.27.

ComfortDelGro (CDG) : The taxi operator posted a 20 per cent fall in net profit to S$141.1 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from S$176.4 million in the previous corresponding period. It said its taxi and private-hire business was hit by competition and cautious consumer spending. Revenue for the nine months rose 4.9 per cent to S$3.94 billion from S$3.75 billion the year before, supported by contracted public transport operations. The company is bidding for more public transport contracts, with opportunities available from 2026 to 2028 estimated at more than S$17 billion. CDG closed flat at S$1.29 on Thursday.

Bumitama : The palm oil producer reported a 2 per cent increase in its net profit to 614 billion rupiah (US$34 million) for the quarter ended Sep 30, 2026, compared with 603 billion rupiah from the corresponding period a year ago. For the nine months ended Sep 30, 2026, net profit rose 31 per cent to 2.4 trillion rupiah from a year ago. The company said its performance was supported by improvements in productivity in its plantations and mills, particularly during the earlier part of the quarter. Shares of Bumitama closed flat at S$1.39 on Thursday.

Food Empire : The company posted an 11.7 per cent rise in revenue to a record US$476.5 million for the nine months ended Sep 30, from US$426.7 million in the previous corresponding period. This was driven mainly by its core Russia and Central Asia segments. For its third quarter ended Sep 30, revenue rose 5.8 per cent to US$161.4 million, from US$152.6 million a year earlier. This was driven by growth across its core segments and partly offset by a 5.2 per cent decline in Europe. Food Empire closed flat at S$1.79 on Thursday.

data.title: Flights grounded across US after air traffic communications outage
data.description:
[WASHINGTON] The US Federal Aviation Administration grounded all departing flights nationwide on Friday (Nov 14) after a communications failure hit air traffic control centers, in only the second such shutdown since the Sep 11, 2001, attacks.

The shutdown caused chaos at airports, with airlines cancelling more than 1,000 flights and delaying nearly 10,000, according to flight-tracking service FlightAware.

Thousands of aircraft already in the air were allowed to land, while those on the ground could not take off. The disruption quickly spread beyond the United States, forcing the cancellation of flights from Canada and Europe.

The Department of Homeland Security said there were no signs the outage was caused by a cyberattack.

“There is no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us. It’s just a telecommunication outage as of right now,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters outside the White House, adding that President Donald Trump had been briefed.

“There’s no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones. This isn’t another 9/11,” Mullin added.

Mullin said the department was examining all possible causes, including a new artificial intelligence-powered air traffic control system.

The disruption is the latest and most dramatic sign of strain on a US air traffic control system beset by equipment and communications failures, controller shortages and aging infrastructure.

Much of the FAA’s air traffic control technology is decades old. Last week, the agency said it would phase out floppy disks used to provide weather and other critical information at more than 400 facilities nationwide by the end of 2028.

From Boston to Seattle and New York to Los Angeles, passengers crowded airport departure halls and airline desks as departure boards filled with delays and cancellations and aircraft remained parked at gates.

“I might cry at some point but not yet,” said Louise Maher, 47, who was still hoping to fly from Newark to London on Friday night despite warnings that her British Airways flight could be delayed by air traffic control restrictions.

The shutdown also left arriving aircraft stranded on taxiways as gates filled up.

Airline officials said the FAA had not indicated when the ground stop might be lifted, but there were preliminary indications the communications issues were improving in some places.

US air traffic woes

The world’s busiest airspace has experienced setbacks in recent years that have disrupted flights and risked safety. In January 2025, a midair collision at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport killed 67 people. The White House and Department of Transportation urged Congress on Friday to approve a further US$30.1 billion to upgrade the United States’ ageing airports and air traffic control system.

The FAA announced the nationwide ground stop at 3:54 pm ET (2054 GMT). At the time the ground stop was issued, 4,042 flights were airborne, destined for US airports, according to Flightradar24. Shortly before the announcement, the FAA halted traffic in Chicago due to air traffic control communications issues.

“If the ground stop continues through the evening, it likely will take the weekend to resolve the disruptions to airlines’ networks,” said Robert Mann, an aviation analyst and principal of R.W. Mann & Co.

The only other nationwide ground stop since the Sep 11 attacks came in January 2023, when the FAA halted domestic departures for less than two hours.

The outage comes amid heightened concern about aviation security worldwide after a wave of hoax bomb threats this month disrupted dozens of passenger flights across Europe, forcing unscheduled landings and prompting fighter jets to escort or intercept aircraft.

There was no immediate indication the US communications failure was related to those incidents.

The US National Weather Service also said on Friday it was experiencing nationwide internet and communications issues. There was no immediate indication the two incidents were connected. REUTERS
